topic: Tối ưu hiệu năng backend trên VPS: Fast-Anything vs rust-anything – Viết lại 5% code nghẽn hay rewrite toàn bộ bằng Rust?

repos.name: fast-anything
repos.description: Don't rewrite it in Rust. Rewrite the 5% that's slow: profile Python, Node or Ruby apps, port the hot functions with your coding agent, prove they behave the same.

repos.name: rust-anything
repos.description: Rewrite your whole app in Rust, one piece at a time, checked against the original's recorded behavior at every step. CLIs, HTTP servers and libraries in TypeScript, Python, C, Go, Ruby and Java.

notes.audience: Backend developers and self-hosters hosting Node.js, Python, or Go workloads on resource-constrained VPS instances who want higher performance without rewriting their entire codebase.
notes.angle: Thay vì mất hàng tháng rewrite toàn bộ backend sang Rust, hãy dùng fast-anything hoặc rust-anything để AI tự tìm và chuyển đúng 5% vòng lặp nghẽn sang Rust giúp tăng tốc gấp chục lần mà không sợ sai logic.

facts.fact: Mỗi hàm được port bởi fast-anything chỉ là một crate chứa một hàm duy nhất nên thời gian biên dịch chỉ mất vài giây thay vì vài phút.
facts.quote: each port is a one-function crate. Seconds, not minutes.

facts.fact: fast-anything kiểm tra tính đúng đắn bằng cách ghi lại tối đa 500 lần gọi thực tế và sinh thêm các trường hợp biên như NaN, vô cùng, chuỗi non-ASCII, input rỗng hoặc lớn gấp 16 lần.
facts.quote: On top of the recorded calls, fast-anything derives extra cases and lets the original answer them: edge cases (NaN, ±infinity, -0.0, zero and ±1, non-ASCII text, empty and up to 16× bigger inputs)

facts.fact: Nếu một bản port Rust chạy đúng nhưng chậm hơn hàm gốc do chi phí chuyển ngữ cảnh (call overhead), fast-anything sẽ từ chối kích hoạt.
facts.quote: A port that is right but slower per call than the original (calling into Rust costs more than the work saved) isn't enabled either.

facts.fact: Trên tác vụ khử trùng lặp mờ (fuzzy dedupe 700 tên) bằng Python, fast-anything giảm thời gian từ 4.91 giây xuống 42ms, đạt mức tăng tốc 116 lần.
Trên TypeScript fuzzy dedupe (2.000 tên), fast-anything giảm từ 3.11 giây xuống 155ms, nhanh hơn 20 lần.
Với các ngôn ngữ như Ruby, Java, Go, PHP, C, C++, C# và R, fast-anything tạo thư viện Rust dùng chuẩn C ABI trao đổi qua JSON mà không đòi hỏi header hay binding phức tạp.
facts.quote: the port is a plain Rust library with one C entry point taking and returning JSON, and fast-anything replays the recorded calls against it directly.

facts.fact: rust-anything cho phép viết lại toàn bộ ứng dụng sang Rust từng phần một, kiểm tra dựa trên hành vi ghi nhận được cho đến khi trở thành ứng dụng thuần Rust bằng lệnh app lift.
facts.quote: When replay passes with no fallback and every unit passes gate, app lift makes it a pure Rust app. The original is never touched.

facts.fact: Thời gian phản hồi đầu tiên của json-server sau khi chuyển sang Rust giảm từ 79-85 ms xuống chỉ còn 8-10 ms.
facts.quote: json-server, from start to first response | 79 to 85 ms | **8 to 10 ms**

facts.fact: Cả hai công cụ đều không tự dịch mã nguồn mà đóng vai trò công cụ định hình cấu trúc, đo lường và xác minh; mã Rust thực tế do coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor...) hoặc lập trình viên viết.
facts.quote: rust-anything does not translate code: your coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, ...) or you write the Rust.

caveats: Cả hai công cụ đều phụ thuộc vào Rust toolchain (rustup) cài sẵn trên hệ thống để biên dịch.

fast-anything chỉ port được các hàm cấp cao nhất (top-level), có tính xác định (deterministic) nhận dữ liệu phẳng (số, chuỗi, danh sách, dict, mảng); không hỗ trợ hàm có logic phụ thuộc trạng thái phức tạp.

rust-anything chạy thử nghiệm nhiều lần trên code gốc khi record: nếu code có tác vụ ghi file, gọi mạng hoặc ghi cơ sở dữ liệu thì các tác vụ này sẽ bị thực thi mỗi lần test, đòi hỏi phải chạy trong môi trường test/staging không có credential thật.
Chỉ tối ưu được những gì tập dữ liệu ghi nhận (recording) bao phủ; các trường hợp chưa được ghi nhận có thể bị bỏ sót.
Đối với mã C/C++, việc viết lại sang Rust bằng rust-anything chủ yếu mang lại độ an toàn bộ nhớ (safety) chứ không hẳn tăng tốc độ thực thi (ví dụ libavutil của ffmpeg có tốc độ tương đương C).
gaps: Chi phí token API cho các LLM coding agent (Claude Code, Codex) khi thực hiện quá trình viết và sửa lỗi mã Rust.
Dung lượng RAM tối thiểu trên VPS để có thể biên dịch mã Rust trực tiếp mà không bị lỗi Out-Of-Memory.
Cách thức deploy tự động các bản vá FFI/C-ABI này lên môi trường CI/CD production của một cụm VPS.

Primary sources, fetched from GitHub on 2026-11-23:

## EL4CTEO/fast-anything (https://github.com/EL4CTEO/fast-anything)
Description: Don't rewrite it in Rust. Rewrite the 5% that's slow: profile Python, Node or Ruby apps, port the hot functions with your coding agent, prove they behave the same.
Homepage: https://www.npmjs.com/package/@el4cteo/fast-anything
Language: Rust; license: MIT; created 2026-11-21; last push 2026-11-23
Latest release: v0.8.0 (2026-11-23)
README (start):
Don't rewrite it in Rust. Rewrite the 5% that's slow.

  

  
  
  
  
  
  
  

Rewriting a whole app in Rust costs months, minute-long compiles and gigabytes of `target/`. Most of the runtime sits in a few functions anyway.

**fast-anything** finds those functions, has your coding agent port *only them* to Rust, proves the port gives the same results on real recorded calls, and swaps it in. One command, fully reversible.

## Install

```sh
npm i -g @el4cteo/fast-anything      # or: cargo install fast-anything
```

Ports are compiled with your Rust toolchain ([rustup](https://rustup.rs)).

## Use

```sh
fast-anything go --agent claude -- python app.py     # or: -- node app.ts / bun app.ts / deno run -A app.ts / ruby app.rb / java App.java / mvn exec:java / gradle run / go run . / php app.php / clang -O2 main.c / Rscript app.R
```

Or step by step:

| command | what it does |
|---|---|
| `scan -- ` | profiles the app, ranks functions by time × how portable they are |
| `port [id]` | records up to 500 real calls, creates a one-function Rust crate + `TASK.md` |
| `verify` | release-builds the port and replays every recorded call |
| `enable` / `disable` | swaps the Rust in or out (one marked block, removed byte for byte) |
| `bench` | times the whole app, original vs Rust, interleaved runs |
| `report` | markdown + SVG card for your PR |
| `doctor` | checks Rust, your runtimes and your agents |

`--agent` takes `claude`, `codex`, or any command that reads a prompt on stdin. Without it, hand `TASK.md` to whatever you use.

## Proof, not vibes

That port looked right but compared bytes instead of characters. 148 of 500 real calls caught it. On top of the recorded calls, fast-anything derives extra cases and lets the original answer them: edge cases (NaN, ±infinity, -0.0, zero and ±1, non-ASCII text, empty and up to 16× bigger inputs) and shrunk inputs (tiny and random slices). Nothing is enabled until every case matches: same values (floats within 1e-9), errors where the original errors. A port that is right but slower per call than the original (calling into Rust costs more than the work saved) isn't enabled either. `FAST_ANYTHING_DISABLE=1` runs the original any time.

## Results

Real runs on an i5-10500, Windows 11 (C and C++: a 4-core GitHub Actions Linux runner). Reproduce them from [`examples/`](examples).

| app | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| Python fuzzy dedupe (700 names) | 4.91s | **42ms, 116×** |
| TypeScript fuzzy dedupe (2,000 names) | 3.11s | **155ms, 20×** |
| PHP fuzzy dedupe (600 names) | 2.94s | **53ms, 55×** |
| Go fuzzy dedupe (3,000 names) | 3.02s | **144ms, 21×** |
| Ruby fuzzy dedupe (400 names) | 3.13s | **228ms, 14×** |
| C# fuzzy dedupe (4,000 names) | 4.03s | **312ms, 13×** |
| Java fuzzy dedupe (4,000 names) | 3.50s | **1.18s, 3×** (11× on the function; the rest is JVM startup) |
| C mandelbrot (8 zoom levels) | 431ms | **127ms, 3.4×** |
| C++ fuzzy dedupe (6,000 names) | 3.02s | **1.09s, 2.7×** |

fast-anything ports the outermost loop it can, not the tiny function called inside it, so the app crosses into Rust once instead of millions of times. Porting only the inner `levenshtein` gave 35× and 1.9×.

## Why not rewrite it all?

- **Compile time**: each port is a one-function crate. Seconds, not minutes.
- **Cache**: every port shares one `.fast/target`. Delete it whenever you like.
- **Risk**: your code stays as it is. Rust is opt-in per function, checked against real behavior.

## Agents

- **Claude Code plugin**: `/plugin marketplace add EL4CTEO/fast-anything`, then `/plugin install fast-anything@fast-anything` and `/fast-anything:fast python app.py`
- **MCP server** (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor…), built into the binary: `claude mcp add fast-anything -- fast-anything mcp`. 8 tools: `fast_scan`, `fast_port`, `fast_verify`, `fast_enable`, `fast_disable`, `fast_bench`, `fast_report`, `fast_status`.
- **Skill**: [`skills/fast-anything`](skills/fast-anything/SKILL.md) teaches any agent the loop.

## Languages

| language | binding | status |
|---|---|---|
| Python 3.10+ | PyO3 | ✅ |
| JavaScript / TypeScript (Node 22+, Bun, Deno 2+: `bun app.ts`, `deno run -A app.ts`) | napi-rs | ✅ |
| Ruby 3.3+ | C ABI + JSON, through Ruby's built-in Fiddle | ✅ |
| Java 22+ (`java App.java`, Maven, Gradle) | the same C bridge, through the FFM API | ✅ |
| Kotlin/JVM (Gradle, `src/main/kotlin`, JDK 22+) | the Java bridge; top-level functions, `object` and companion members, extension functions | ✅ |
| Go 1.22+ (`go run .`) | the same C bridge, through the Windows loader or dlopen (cgo) | ✅ |
| PHP 8.1+ (`php app.php`) | the same C bridge, through PHP's FFI extension (`extension=ffi`) | ✅ |
| C and C++ (gcc, clang or Intel oneAPI icx/icpx: `clang -O2 main.c lib.c`) | the same C bridge, through LoadLibrary or dlopen | ✅ |
| C# / .NET 8+ (`dotnet run -c Release`) | the same C bridge, through NativeLibrary; profiled with EventPipe, nothing to install | ✅ |
| R 4.0+ (`Rscript app.R`) | the same C bridge, through base R's `.C()`; profiled with Rprof, no packages or R headers needed | ✅ |

It ports top-level, deterministic functions that take plain data (numbers, strings, lists, dicts, typed arrays…), including ones in your entry script when its main code sits under `if __name__ == "__main__":` (or `if __FILE__ == $0`, or `if (import.meta.main)` / `if (require.main === module)`). In Python that means module-level functions and `@staticmethod`s (dataclasses, NamedTuples and numeric NumPy arrays count as plain data), in Java, C# and PHP static methods (and PHP functions), in Go plain functions, in C and C++ free functions and static methods. `scan` says why anything else can't move yet.

With Intel oneAPI on Windows, run fast-anything from a shell where `setvars.bat` ran (it sets up the linker). SYCL kernels run on the device and aren't ported; with `-fsycl`, only host functions are profiled and ported.

Ruby, Java, Go, PHP, C, C++, C# and R need no headers, bindings or extra tools: the port is a plain Rust library with one C entry point taking and returning JSON, and fast-anything replays the recorded calls against it directly. Any language that can call C can use that bridge.

## License

MIT

## erkamyaman/rust-anything (https://github.com/erkamyaman/rust-anything)
Description: Rewrite your whole app in Rust, one piece at a time, checked against the original's recorded behavior at every step. CLIs, HTTP servers and libraries in TypeScript, Python, C, Go, Ruby and Java.
Homepage: https://www.npmjs.com/package/rust-anything
Language: Rust; license: MIT; created 2026-11-16; last push 2026-11-22
Latest release: v3.3.0 (2026-11-22)
README (start):
rust-anything

English · Türkçe · Українська · 简体中文 · 繁體中文 · Deutsch · Français · Русский · 日本語 · 한국어 · Azərbaycanca · Oʻzbekcha · Қазақша · Кыргызча · Türkmençe · Татарча · ئۇيغۇرچە · Português · Tiếng Việt · Español · Italiano

Rewrite your app in Rust, and prove it still behaves the same.
Point it at your app: it records what the original does, your coding agent writes the Rust one piece at a time,
and every piece is checked against that recording before it moves on. It doesn't translate code; it proves the rewrite.

  
  
  
  
  
  
  
  
  
  

Install · Releases · Claude Code plugin · MCP Registry · Real-world ports · FAQ
Languages · How it works · Whole apps · Sponsors · MIT
Made in Türkiye 🇹🇷 by erKam Yaman · ❤️ Sponsor me · Sponsored by  CodeRabbit

New in 2.0: Prettier, ported to Rust. 19x faster · 15,861 of 17,224 recorded runs fully in Rust · every run byte-identical

  
  
  Prettier against its Rust port on 59 real files from ms, Fuse.js and json-server (Apple M4). Same output, byte for byte. How it was measured.

PHP and C#: unit ports, through FFI and P/Invoke.

  
    
      Record
      record runs the original on generated edge cases, semantic traps and your own inputs, and saves what it returns or throws.
    
    
      Port
      bridge generates the Rust crate and a wrapper, so callers keep the original API. You or your agent write the Rust.
    
    
      Check
      diff replays every recorded case against the Rust, and nothing ships until they all match and gate passes.
    
    
      Lift
      When replay passes with no fallback and every unit passes gate, app lift makes it a pure Rust app. The original is never touched.
    
  

**Rewrite your whole app in Rust, one piece at a time.** rust-anything records what your
Node.js (TypeScript/JavaScript), Python, C, Go, Ruby, Java or Kotlin app does today, then checks every piece of the
Rust rewrite against that recording before it moves on, until the app is pure Rust. CLIs, HTTP
servers and libraries; your coding agent (or you) writes the Rust. It is built on
[napi-rs](https://github.com/napi-rs/napi-rs), [PyO3](https://github.com/PyO3/pyo3) and
[wasm-bindgen](https://github.com/wasm-bindgen/wasm-bindgen), which carry the calls between your
language and Rust; rust-anything decides what to move and proves it matches. It can only catch what the
recording covers: see [What it can't catch](docs/how-it-works.md#what-it-cant-catch). Whole tools
and servers, or only the slow part, one hot path at a time:

| Real project, same output as the original | Original | With rust-anything |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| [Prettier](docs/real-world.md#prettier) 3.6.2, 2,360 JS/TS files from the command line | 128.6 s | **6.9 s: 19x faster** |
| Prettier, 6,305 Markdown files from the command line | 352 s | **22.5 s: 15.6x faster** |
| [json-server](docs/real-world.md#json-server), a whole Node server: memory at idle | 74 MB | **3.5 MB**, one 5.3 MB binary |
| json-server, from start to first response | 79 to 85 ms | **8 to 10 ms** |
| [Fuse.js](docs/real-world.md#fusejs) search over 50,000 strings, per query | 91.2 ms | **2.8 ms: 32x faster** |

Prettier: 15,861 of 17,224 recorded runs format fully in Rust across 10 languages (JavaScript,
TypeScript, JSX, JSON, GraphQL, YAML, Markdown, CSS, SCSS, Less), and all 17,224 match Prettier
byte for byte, since anything not ported yet falls back to Prettier. json-server: 514/514
recorded HTTP cases match on a pure Rust binary. Measured on an Apple M4, two runs each, every
output compared before timing ([details](docs/real-world.md)). Calling Rust once per small
function is usually *slower* than a JIT; rust-anything finds the loop worth moving, and moves it. Against
C the win is safety, not speed: [ffmpeg's libavutil](docs/real-world.md#ffmpeg) ported to Rust
matches all 226,447 recorded calls and runs at about C's speed (18 of 42 benchmarks even, 8
faster, 16 slower by 3 to 40%).

## Only the slow part

You don't have to port the whole app. Point `go` at a command that is too slow, and it ports
the one function that takes the time:

```sh
rust-anything go --agent claude -- python3 app.py
```

It profiles the run, picks the outermost function worth moving (the loop, not the small call
inside it, batched where the profile says so), records it on generated inputs plus the calls your
run makes, and hands `src/port.rs` to your agent (`claude`, `codex`, or any command that reads a
prompt on stdin; without `--agent` it writes `TASK.md` for you and stops). It switches the
function on only when every recorded case matches and `gate` passes. Then:

```sh
rust-anything report rust/dedupe-rs     # REPORT.md and card.svg for the pull request
rust-anything disable rust/dedupe-rs    # back to the original, byte for byte
```

The [Fuse.js](docs/real-world.md#fusejs) row above is this shape: Fuse's score for one string,
batched over the list, moved to Rust while object keys, extended search and the rest stay in
JavaScript, for 91.2 ms to 2.8 ms per query over 50,000 strings. Try `go` on
[`tests/fixtures/go-fuzzy`](tests/fixtures/go-fuzzy), a 20-line Python dedupe. Every way to switch
a port on and off: [Switch a port on and off](docs/how-it-works.md#switch-a-port-on-and-off).

  
  
  json-server, a whole Node server, lifted to a pure Rust binary (Apple M4). How it was measured.

> rust-anything is an independent project, not affiliated with or endorsed by the Rust Project
> or the Rust Foundation. "Rust" is a trademark of the Rust Foundation.

> [!WARNING]
> `record` and `app record` run your original code, calling each function (or the whole app) on
> many generated inputs, and `app record` runs every case twice. `diff`, `gate` and `app replay`
> run the same cases again, on the port or the original. Code that writes files, talks to a
> database or calls the network does that once per case. Run them on a copy of the project, with a
> test database and no production credentials in the environment.

## Install the ports

The ESLint port is an npm command. It runs the Rust port for what it covers and ESLint 10.15.0,
pinned as a dependency, for everything else, so the output is ESLint's either way:

```sh
npm install -g eslint-rs     # ESLint 10.15.0
```

| Command | Answered in Rust | Handed to ESLint 10.15.0 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `eslint-rs` | `--no-config-lookup --rule ... --stdin` with the 90 ported rules (`stylish` and `json` output, fixes, suggestions) | `eslint.config.*` lookups (`eslint .`), files and folders, the other 202 core rules, plugins, parsers, the other formatters, parse errors |

The binary comes for macOS (arm64, x64) and Linux (x64, arm64, glibc). On Windows and elsewhere,
or with `RUST_ANYTHING_MODE=old`, `eslint-rs` runs ESLint itself: same output, no speedup.
Installed from its tarballs on macOS arm64, `eslint-rs` matches ESLint 10.15.0 installed beside it
on all 10,585 recorded runs ([how](docs/packaging.md#a-whole-cli-front-door)).

The Prettier port is packaged the same way (`prettier-rs`, Prettier 3.6.2) and replays
17,224/17,224 recorded runs from its tarballs, 7.9% handed to Prettier, but it is not on npm.
`rust-anything package` makes this kind of package from any CLI front door.

## Quick start

Paste this into Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI or OpenCode and let your agent install it:

```text
Install rust-anything: run `cargo install rust-anything`, then `rust-anything setup`.
Tell me when to restart you.
```

Or yourself:

```sh
cargo install rust-anything   # from crates.io
rust-anything setup           # registers it with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI and OpenCode
```

No Rust toolchain yet? Prebuilt binaries for macOS, Linux and Windows are attached to each
[GitHub release](https://github.com/erkamyaman/rust-anything/releases), and for JavaScript
projects `npm install -g rust-anything` installs the same binary.

In Claude Code you can also install it as a plugin (the MCP server and the skill; the CLI above
must be on your `PATH`):

```text
/plugin install rust-anything --marketplace erkamyaman/rust-anything
```

In Codex, from the agents marketplace in this repo (`.agents/plugins/marketplace.json`, the same
plugin under `plugin/`, with the skill and MCP server):

```sh
codex plugin marketplace add erkamyaman/rust-anything
codex plugin add rust-anything@rust-anything
```

`setup` adds the MCP server to each agent it finds and installs the workflow skill where the agent
reads skills. It keeps your other settings, is safe to run again, and `--remove` undoes it.
Then ask your agent, for example:

- *"Rewrite this CLI in Rust with rust-anything, end to end, and prove it behaves the same."*
- *"This search feels slow. Profile it with rust-anything and move the hot loop to Rust."*
- *"Plan a migration of `src/parser/` to Rust with rust-anything; port the first unit and prove it."*
- *"Bench the Rust port in `rust/text-rs` against the original and tell me whether to ship it."*

### Works with

| Agent | `rust-anything setup` adds |
| --- | --- |
| Claude Code | MCP server in `~/.claude.json`, skill in `~/.claude/skills/` |
| Codex | MCP server in `~/.codex/config.toml`, skill in `~/.codex/skills/` |
| Cursor | MCP server in `~/.cursor/mcp.json` |
| Gemini CLI | MCP server in `~/.gemini/settings.json` |
| OpenCode | MCP server in `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json` (`mcp.servers`), skill in `~/.config/opencode/skills/` |
| Any other MCP client | add `rust-anything mcp` as a stdio server by hand (see [Install](docs/install.md#install)) |

Before changing a file that exists, `setup` saves a copy beside it (`.rust-anything.bak`); `--no-backup` skips the copy.

To wire OpenCode up by hand, put the server in `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json` (`command` is
the whole argv) and copy [`skills/rust-anything/`](./skills/rust-anything) to
`~/.config/opencode/skills/rust-anything/`:

```json
{
  "mcp": {
    "servers": {
      "rust-anything": { "type": "local", "command": ["rust-anything", "mcp"] }
    }
  }
}
```

Or run the steps yourself:

```sh
rust-anything profile . -- node bench.mjs              # what is hot, and who calls it
rust-anything bridge . src/fuzzy.ts --batch fuzzyScore:text
# write src/port.rs (or let your agent), then:
rust-anything record rust/fuzzy-rs && rust-anything build rust/fuzzy-rs
rust-anything diff rust/fuzzy-rs                       # every recorded case must match
rust-anything fuzz rust/fuzzy-rs --time 60 --keep      # fresh inputs: what the recording missed
rust-anything bench rust/fuzzy-rs                      # faster? the verdict says
rust-anything gate rust/fuzzy-rs                       # done means this passes
```

rust-anything does not translate code: your coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, ...) or you write
the Rust. rust-anything supplies what an agent cannot guess reliably: where the time goes, what to port
first and in which order, a bridge so the rest of the code calls the Rust with its API unchanged,
the exact behavior the port must match, a safe way to ship it, and a gate that says when a port is
done.

Same output is not enough. Record what the app sends too, and a rewrite that mails twice fails:

  
  
  A real run of app record --effects and app replay. See Side effects.

## Languages

| Language | Unit | Bridge | Recorded and replayed by |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| TypeScript/JavaScript | folder or file | napi-rs or wasm-bindgen with a generated binary wire; classes and async included | Node, running the `.ts` sources |
| Python | package or module | PyO3 (abi3), direct conversion, typed exceptions | Python, importing the original |
| C | `.c` file | `extern "C"` functions with the original names and a header | the original compiled to a shared library, called through ctypes, one fork per case |
| Go | package | typed cgo calls and a generated binary wire, in a package with the original API | a generated Go driver, built as its own module |

## therealaleph/MasterHttpRelayVPN-RUST (https://github.com/therealaleph/MasterHttpRelayVPN-RUST)

# mhrv-rs — bypass censorship for free, with your own Google account

[](https://github.com/therealaleph/MasterHttpRelayVPN-RUST/releases/latest)
[](https://github.com/therealaleph/MasterHttpRelayVPN-RUST/releases)

**A small program that runs on your computer and lets you visit blocked websites for free, using a Google Apps Script you deploy in your own free Google account. Your ISP only sees encrypted traffic to `www.google.com` — it can't tell what you're really visiting.**

🇬🇧 [English Quick Start](#quick-start) · [Full Guide (advanced topics)](docs/guide.md)
🇮🇷 [راه‌اندازی سریع فارسی](#راه‌اندازی-سریع) · [راهنمای کامل (مباحث پیشرفته)](docs/guide.fa.md)

  ۱. راهنمای تصویری راه اندازی به زبان فارسی (YouTube)
  
  ۲. راهنمای جامع متنی راه اندازی به زبان فارسی با تشکر از Kian Irani

---

## What you get

- 🌐 **Bypasses DPI / SNI blocking** by using Google's edge as a relay
- 💯 **Completely free** — runs on your own Google account's free tier
- ⚡ **One small file** (~3 MB), no Python, no Node.js, no dependencies
- 🖥️ **Works on** Mac, Windows, Linux, Android, OpenWRT routers
- 🦊 **Any browser or app** that supports HTTP proxy or SOCKS5

## How it works (the simple picture)

```
   you  →  browser  →  mhrv-rs  ──┐
                                  │ ISP only sees:  www.google.com
                                  ▼
                          Google's network
                                  │
                                  ▼
              your free Apps Script  fetches  the real site
                                  │
                                  ▼
                Twitter / ChatGPT / blocked-site of your choice
```

ISPs can't read inside encrypted HTTPS. They only see the address — `www.google.com`. The actual page lookup happens inside Google's network, hidden in the encrypted tunnel.

## Quick Start

**About 5 minutes.** You need:

- A free Google account (any Gmail works)
- A computer (Mac, Windows, or Linux)
- Firefox or Chrome

### Step 1 — Make the Google Apps Script (one-time)

1. Go to **[script.google.com](https://script.google.com)**, sign in with your Google account
2. Click **New project** at the top left
3. Delete the default code in the editor
4. Open the file [`assets/apps_script/Code.gs`](assets/apps_script/Code.gs) in this repo, copy all of it, paste into the Apps Script editor (replacing what was there)
5. Find this line near the top:
   ```js
   const AUTH_KEY = "CHANGE_ME_TO_A_STRONG_SECRET";
   ```
   Change `CHANGE_ME_TO_A_STRONG_SECRET` to a long random string of your own. **Keep this string** — you'll paste it into the app in Step 3. Treat it like a password.
6. Click 💾 **Save** (or `Ctrl/Cmd+S`)
7. Click **Deploy** (top right) → **New deployment**
8. Click the gear icon ⚙ next to "Select type" → choose **Web app**
9. Set:
   - **Execute as:** *Me* (your Google account)
   - **Who has access:** *Anyone*
10. Click **Deploy**. Google may ask for permissions — click **Authorize access** and approve
11. Google shows a **Deployment ID** (a long random string). **Copy it** — you'll need it in Step 3.

> **Tip:** if you ever update `Code.gs` later, don't make a new deployment. Edit the code, then go to **Deploy → Manage deployments → ✏️ → Version: New version → Deploy**. The Deployment ID stays the same.

### Step 2 — Download mhrv-rs

Go to the [latest release page](https://github.com/therealaleph/MasterHttpRelayVPN-RUST/releases/latest) and download the file for your computer:

| You're on | Download this |
|---|---|
| Mac with Apple Silicon (M1 / M2 / M3 / M4 chip) | `mhrv-rs-macos-arm64-app.zip` |
| Mac with Intel chip | `mhrv-rs-macos-amd64-app.zip` |
| Windows | `mhrv-rs-windows-amd64.zip` |
| Linux (Ubuntu / Mint / Fedora / Debian / Arch) | `mhrv-rs-linux-amd64.tar.gz` |
| Android phone or tablet | `mhrv-rs-android-universal-v*.apk` |
| OpenWRT router or Alpine | `mhrv-rs-linux-musl-amd64.tar.gz` |

> **Mac: not sure if Apple Silicon or Intel?** Click  → **About This Mac**. If "Chip" says **Apple**, get arm64. If **Intel**, get amd64.

> **Linux: getting a `GLIBC` error?** Use the `linux-musl-amd64` file instead — it works on any Linux without dependencies.

Unzip it.

### Step 3 — First run

Double-click the launcher:

| Mac | `run.command` |
| Windows | `run.bat` |
| Linux | `./run.sh` (in a terminal) |

The first time, it asks for your computer password. This is to install one small certificate so your browser trusts mhrv-rs. **The certificate is generated on your computer and never leaves it** — no cloud, no Google, nothing remote can use it.

The mhrv-rs window opens. Fill in:

- **Apps Script ID(s)** → paste the **Deployment ID** from Step 1
- **Auth key** → paste the random string you put in `Code.gs`
- Leave everything else at the defaults

Click **Save config

One nice feature is that this crate allows you to build add-ons purely with the Rust/JavaScript toolchain and without involving node-gyp.

Taste

You can start from package-template to play with napi-rs

Define JavaScript functions
use napi::bindgen_prelude::*;
use napi_derive::napi;

/// module registration is done by the runtime, no need to explicitly do it now.
#[napi]
pub fn fibonacci(n: u32) -> u32 {
  match n {
    1 | 2 => 1,
    _ => fibonacci(n - 1) + fibonacci(n - 2),
  }
}

/// use `Fn`, `FnMut` or `FnOnce` traits to defined JavaScript callbacks
/// the return type of callbacks can only be `Result`.
#[napi]
pub fn get_cwd<T: Fn(String) -> Result<()>>(callback: T) {
  callback(
    std::env::current_dir()
      .unwrap()
      .to_string_lossy()
      .to_string(),
  )
  .unwrap();
}

/// or, define the callback signature in where clause
#[napi]
pub fn test_callback<T>(callback: T) -> Result<()>
where
  T: Fn(String) -> Result<()>,
{
  callback(std::env::current_dir()?.to_string_lossy().to_string())
}

/// async fn, require `async` feature enabled.
/// [dependencies]
/// napi = {version="2", features=["async"]}
#[napi]
pub async fn read_file_async(path: String) -> Result<Buffer> {
  Ok(tokio::fs::read(path).await?.into())
}

more examples at examples

Building

This repository is a Cargo crate. Any napi-based add-on should contain Cargo.toml to make it a Cargo crate.

In your Cargo.toml you need to set the crate-type to "cdylib" so that cargo builds a C-style shared library that can be dynamically loaded by the Node executable. You'll also need to add this crate as a dependency.

[package]
name = "awesome"

[lib]
crate-type = ["cdylib"]

[dependencies]
napi = "3"
napi-derive = "3"

[build-dependencies]
napi-build = "2"

And create build.rs in your own project:

// build.rs
extern crate napi_build;

fn main() {
  napi_build::setup();
}

So far, the napi build script has only been tested on macOS Linux Windows x64 MSVC and FreeBSD.

Install @napi-rs/cli as a local development dependency to build the Rust crate and copy its dynamic library to a loadable .node file.

{
  "name": "awesome-package",
  "devDependencies": {
    "@napi-rs/cli": "^3.0.0"
  },
  "napi": {
    "binaryName": "jarvis"
  },
  "scripts": {
    "build": "napi build --release",
    "build:debug": "napi build"
  }
}

Then you can require your native binding:

require('./jarvis.node')

The module_name would be your package name in your Cargo.toml.

xxx => ./xxx.node

xxx-yyy => ./xxx_yyy.node

You can also copy Dynamic lib file to an appointed location:

napi build [--release] ./dll
napi build [--release] ./artifacts

There are documents which contains more details about the @napi-rs/cli usage.

wasm32-wasip1-threads allocator lock

On wasm32-wasip1-threads, napi takes one lock around every call into wasi-libc's allocator and refreshes the calling thread's view of the shared memory size under it. This works around a V8 bug: a thread keeps a stale memory size after another thread grows the shared memory, and can trap with "memory access out of bounds" on the new pages. The heap also stays below 2 GiB: an allocation that would pass it fails, because Node's WASI rejects pointers at or above 2 GiB. napi_build::setup() adds the link arguments this needs. Opt out with --cfg napi_wasi_no_heap_sync in the target rustflags; see napi-build. The lock cost 3-11% on rolldown's loads; the numbers, the napi_wasm_heap_sync_stat test counters and what the lock does not cover are in the WASI docs.

Testing

Because libraries that depend on this crate must be loaded into a Node executable in order to resolve symbols, all tests are written in JavaScript in the test_module subdirectory.

To run tests:

yarn build:test
yarn test

PyO3

      

Rust bindings for Python, including tools for creating native Python extension modules. Running and interacting with Python code from a Rust binary is also supported.

User Guide: stable | main

API Documentation: stable | main

Usage

Requires Rust 1.85 or greater.

PyO3 supports the following Python distributions:

CPython 3.9 or greater
PyPy 7.3 (Python 3.11+)
GraalPy 25.4 or greater (Python 3.13+)

You can use PyO3 to write a native Python module in Rust, or to embed Python in a Rust binary. The following sections explain each of these in turn.

Using Rust from Python

PyO3 can be used to generate a native Python module. The easiest way to try this out for the first time is to use maturin. maturin is a tool for building and publishing Rust-based Python packages with minimal configuration. The following steps install maturin, use it to generate and build a new Python package, and then launch Python to import and execute a function from the package.

First, follow the commands below to create a new directory containing a new Python virtualenv, and install maturin into the virtualenv using Python's package manager, pip:

# (replace string_sum with the desired package name)
$ mkdir string_sum
$ cd string_sum
$ python -m venv .env
$ source .env/bin/activate
$ pip install maturin

Still inside this string_sum directory, now run maturin init. This will generate the new package source. When given the choice of bindings to use, select pyo3 bindings:

$ maturin init
✔ 🤷 What kind of bindings to use? · pyo3
  ✨ Done! New project created string_sum

The most important files generated by this command are Cargo.toml and lib.rs, which will look roughly like the following:

Cargo.toml

[package]
name = "string_sum"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2024"

[lib]
# The name of the native library. This is the name which will be used in Python to import the
# library (i.e. `import string_sum`). If you change this, you must also change the name of the
# `#[pymodule]` in `src/lib.rs`.
name = "string_sum"
# "cdylib" is necessary to produce a shared library for Python to import from.
#
# Downstream Rust code (including code in `bin/`, `examples/`, and `tests/`) will not be able
# to `use string_sum;` unless the "rlib" or "lib" crate type is also included, e.g.:
# crate-type = ["cdylib", "rlib"]
crate-type = ["cdylib"]

[dependencies]
pyo3 = "0.30.0"

src/lib.rs

/// A Python module implemented in Rust. The name of this module must match
/// the `lib.name` setting in the `Cargo.toml`, else Python will not be able to
/// import the module.
#[pyo3::pymodule]
mod string_sum {
  use pyo3::prelude::*;

  /// Formats the sum of two numbers as string.
  #[pyfunction]
  fn sum_as_string(a: usize, b: usize) -> PyResult<String> {
    Ok((a + b).to_string())
  }
}

Finally, run maturin develop. This will build the package and install it into the Python virtualenv previously created and activated. The package is then ready to be used from python:

$ maturin develop
# lots of progress output as maturin runs the compilation...
$ python
>>> import string_sum
>>> string_sum.sum_as_string(5, 20)
'25'

When checking runtime performance, run maturin develop --release to build with optimizations.

To make changes to the package, just edit the Rust source code and then re-run maturin develop to recompile.

To run this all as a single copy-and-paste, use the bash script below (replace string_sum in the first command with the desired package name):

mkdir string_sum && cd "$_"
python -m venv .env
source .env/bin/activate
pip install maturin
maturin init --bindings pyo3
maturin develop

If you want to be able to run cargo test or use this project in a Cargo workspace and are running into linker issues, there are some workarounds in the FAQ.

As well as with maturin, it is possible to build using setuptools-rust or manually. Both offer more flexibility than maturin but require more configuration to get started.

Using Python from Rust

To embed Python into a Rust binary, you need to ensure that your Python installation contains a shared library. The following steps demonstrate how to ensure this (for Ubuntu), and then give some example code which runs an embedded Python interpreter.

To install the Python shared library on Ubuntu:

sudo apt install python3-dev

To install the Python shared library on RPM based distributions (e.g. Fedora, Red Hat, SuSE), install the python3-devel package.

Start a new project with cargo new and add pyo3 to the Cargo.toml like this:

[dependencies.pyo3]
version = "0.30.0"
# Enabling this cargo feature will cause PyO3 to start a Python interpreter on first call to `Python::attach`
features = ["auto-initialize"]

Example program displaying the value of sys.version and the current user name:

use pyo3::prelude::*;
use pyo3::types::IntoPyDict;

fn main() -> PyResult<()> {
    Python::attach(|py| {
        let sys = py.import("sys")?;
        let version: String = sys.getattr("version")?.extract()?;

        let locals = [("os", py.import("os")?)].into_py_dict(py)?;
        let code = c"os.getenv('USER') or os.getenv('USERNAME') or 'Unknown'";
        let user: String = py.eval(code, None, Some(&locals))?.extract()?;

        println!("Hello {}, I'm Python {}", user, version);
        Ok(())
    })
}

The guide has a section with lots of examples about this topic.
